questions.stem: Free and competitive markets tend to promote allocative efficiency because:
options: governments direct resources to the industries that need them most urgently
firms can set their prices well above cost without losing any customers
each firm produces every good and service that consumers might want
prices signal what consumers value, guiding resources to those uses
questions.explanation: In a competitive market, prices rise where consumers value goods more, raising profits and drawing resources into those uses. This happens through the price mechanism rather than government direction.

questions.stem: Competition between firms is most likely to improve productive efficiency because:
options: competition raises prices, which increases profits available for investment
consumers must pay whatever price the largest firm in the market decides
firms with higher costs than rivals lose sales and must cut costs or leave
firms in the same industry can share their costs and agree on output levels
questions.explanation: Competitive pressure forces firms to minimise costs, since a high-cost firm cannot charge more than its rivals and stay in the market. Agreements to share costs or set output reduce competition rather than reflect it.

questions.stem: A free and competitive market helps raise material living standards mainly because:
options: it ensures private firms supply public goods such as national defence and street lighting
it prevents any resources from being left unemployed at any stage of the business cycle
lower prices and greater choice let consumers buy more goods and services with their incomes
it guarantees that income is distributed equally across all the households in the economy
questions.explanation: Competition pushes prices towards costs and encourages firms to offer variety and quality, so real incomes stretch further. Markets do not guarantee an equal distribution of income, and they tend to under-provide public goods.

questions.stem: Market failure occurs when:
options: firms make a loss and leave the industry
the government imposes a tax in a market
the free market does not allocate resources in the way that maximises society's welfare
the market price of a good rises above what some consumers are willing to pay for it
questions.explanation: Market failure means the price mechanism, left to itself, produces an allocation of resources that is not efficient for society, as with public goods or externalities. A price some buyers cannot afford, or a firm leaving an industry, is a normal part of how markets work.

questions.stem: Public goods are characterised by being:
options: non-excludable and non-rival in consumption
excludable and rival in consumption
non-excludable but rival in consumption
provided by the government and funded from taxation
questions.explanation: A public good is one that people cannot be stopped from using and whose use by one person does not reduce what is available to others. Goods that are non-excludable but rival are common access resources, and many government-provided services are not public goods at all.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a pure public good?
options: A trip on a privately run toll road
A lighthouse that guides every ship passing a stretch of coast
A bed in a public hospital
A place in a government secondary school
questions.explanation: Ships cannot be excluded from a lighthouse's light, and one ship's use does not reduce its usefulness to others. Hospital beds, school places and toll roads are rival or excludable, even when government provides them.

questions.stem: The free market tends to under-provide public goods mainly because:
options: consumers place little or no value on public goods such as street lighting
public goods are rival, so one person's use leaves less for everyone else to use
people can benefit without paying, so firms cannot charge enough to cover their costs
public goods are too expensive for private firms to produce at any scale of output, whatever the demand
questions.explanation: Because no one can be excluded, people have an incentive to free ride, so private firms cannot collect enough revenue to supply public goods. Public goods are non-rival, and people often value them highly.

questions.stem: One more household's use of the national weather forecasting service does not reduce the service available to anyone else. This property is called:
options: a positive production externality
asymmetric information
non-rivalry in consumption
non-excludability
questions.explanation: Non-rivalry means one person's consumption does not reduce what is left for others. Non-excludability is the separate property that people cannot be prevented from using the good.

questions.stem: An externality is:
options: a cost borne by an Australian firm when it exports its goods and services overseas
a benefit a consumer receives from buying a good at a discounted price
a tax placed by the government on goods produced outside Australia
a cost or benefit of production or consumption that falls on a third party
questions.explanation: Externalities are spillover costs or benefits that affect people who are neither the buyer nor the seller. Because they are not reflected in the market price, the market produces too much or too little of the good.

questions.stem: A factory discharges waste into a river used downstream by farmers. Without government intervention, the market for the factory's product will:
options: under-allocate resources to it, as its price is above the full social cost of producing it
allocate resources efficiently, as the farmers are not buyers of the factory's product
over-allocate resources to it, because demand for the product is price inelastic
over-allocate resources to it, as its price does not reflect the full social cost
questions.explanation: The cost to the farmers is a negative externality the factory does not pay, so its private costs are below the social cost. The product is therefore priced too low and overproduced compared with the efficient level.

questions.stem: Vaccination is said to create a positive externality because:
options: vaccine producers earn profits from the sale of each dose
the government pays for most vaccines through the budget
it costs the patient less than the treatment it prevents
it lowers the risk of disease for people who are not vaccinated themselves
questions.explanation: A positive externality is a benefit to third parties, and vaccination reduces the spread of disease to others. Lower treatment costs for the patient are a private benefit, not a spillover.

questions.stem: Left to the free market, goods that create positive externalities, such as education, tend to be:
options: under-produced, as buyers ignore the benefits to third parties
over-produced, as private benefits are greater than social benefits
produced at the efficient level, as consumers pay the full price
under-produced, as their social benefit is below their private benefit
questions.explanation: When a good has positive externalities, its social benefit exceeds the private benefit buyers consider. Buyers demand only enough to match their own benefit, so the market supplies less than the socially efficient quantity.

questions.stem: In the market for coal-fired electricity, the social cost of production exceeds the private cost. Compared with the socially efficient outcome, the free market produces:
options: too much electricity at too high a price
too little electricity at too low a price
too much electricity at too low a price
too little electricity at too high a price
questions.explanation: Producers ignore the external cost, so their supply curve sits below the social cost curve. The market price is lower and the quantity higher than if the full social cost were reflected in price.

questions.stem: Asymmetric information exists when:
options: buyers and sellers are both unsure about a product's quality
prices for the same good differ between two different markets
a firm advertises its product to some consumers but not others
one party to a transaction knows more than the other
questions.explanation: Asymmetric information is an imbalance of knowledge between the parties to a transaction. It can lead people to make choices they would not make with full information, so resources are misallocated.

questions.stem: The seller of a used car knows it has a faulty gearbox, but the buyer does not. This is an example of:
options: a common access resource being overused
the free-rider problem associated with public goods
asymmetric information leading to market failure
a negative production externality on the buyer
questions.explanation: The seller knows more than the buyer about the car's quality, so the buyer may pay more than the car is worth. The cost falls on a party to the transaction, so it is not an externality on a third party.

questions.stem: Insurers cannot tell how carefully each driver drives, so they set premiums at an average level. Careful drivers may then decide cover is poor value and not buy it. This problem arises from:
options: the public good nature of motor vehicle insurance
the income effect of an increase in insurance premiums
asymmetric information between insurers and drivers
a negative consumption externality from careless driving
questions.explanation: Drivers know more about their own risk than insurers do, so premiums cannot be matched to risk. Low-risk drivers drop out, leaving a riskier pool, which is a market failure caused by unequal information.

questions.stem: Which intervention most directly addresses asymmetric information in the market for financial advice?
options: Setting a maximum price that financial advisers may charge for each meeting with a client
Requiring advisers to disclose their fees and conflicts of interest to clients
Placing an indirect tax on each financial product sold to retail clients
Subsidising the cost of financial advice for every household that seeks it
questions.explanation: Disclosure rules give clients the information advisers already have, which reduces the imbalance of knowledge. Taxes, subsidies and price limits change prices, but they do not give clients better information.

questions.stem: Laws requiring that packaged food labels list ingredients and nutritional content mainly address:
options: asymmetric information between food producers and consumers
a negative production externality from food manufacturing
the under-provision of food as a public good
the overuse of a common access resource
questions.explanation: Producers know what is in their products, while shoppers cannot easily check, so labelling rules close the information gap. Food is rival and excludable, so it is not a public good.

questions.stem: A common access resource is one that is:
options: non-rival and non-excludable in consumption
excludable and rival in consumption
owned by the government and sold to private firms
rival in consumption but non-excludable
questions.explanation: With a common access resource, such as an open fishery, people cannot be excluded, but each unit used leaves less for others. That combination leads to overuse, unlike a public good, which is non-rival.

questions.stem: An open-access fishery is likely to be overfished because:
options: fishers have perfect information about fish stocks and choose to run them down
each fisher gains from catching more, but the cost of depleted stocks is shared by all
fish are non-rival, so one boat's catch leaves the same stock for every other boat
the price of fish is too high for consumers, so fishers must increase their catch
questions.explanation: Each fisher keeps the full benefit of extra catch but bears only a small share of the cost of a shrinking stock, so all fish too much. Fish are rival, since a fish caught by one boat cannot be caught by another.

questions.stem: Farmers draw water from a shared underground basin faster than it recharges, leaving less for future users. This mainly reflects a loss of:
options: productive efficiency, as farmers waste water on each crop they grow
dynamic efficiency, as farmers are slow to switch to different crops
allocative efficiency, as the water in the basin is a pure public good
intertemporal efficiency, as future users' needs are not considered
questions.explanation: The basin is a common access resource, and each farmer ignores the cost of depletion to future users, so resources are not balanced over time. Water in the basin is rival, so it is not a public good.

questions.stem: Indirect taxes, such as excise on alcohol, are levied on:
options: the personal incomes of workers and investors
the market value of property that people own
the profits that companies earn over a year
the sale or production of goods and services
questions.explanation: An indirect tax is collected on spending on goods and services and is usually passed on in the price. Taxes on incomes and profits are direct taxes.

questions.stem: The government raises the excise on cigarettes. In the cigarette market:
options: supply shifts right, price falls and quantity traded rises
supply shifts left, price rises and quantity traded rises
supply shifts left, price rises and quantity traded falls
demand shifts left, price falls and quantity traded falls
questions.explanation: Excise adds to producers' costs for each unit sold, reducing supply at every price. The leftward shift of supply raises the market price and lowers the quantity traded.

questions.stem: Demand for tobacco is price inelastic. An increase in tobacco excise is therefore likely to:
options: raise substantial revenue but reduce consumption only modestly
reduce consumption sharply but raise little extra tax revenue
lower the price that smokers pay for each packet of cigarettes
shift the demand curve for tobacco products to the left
questions.explanation: With inelastic demand, the quantity bought falls by a smaller proportion than the price rises, so most sales continue and the tax raises much revenue. The tax shifts supply, not demand, and it raises the price paid by smokers.

questions.stem: The main purpose of a tax on a good that creates a negative externality is to:
options: increase consumption of goods that are complements to the good being taxed
make its price reflect the full social cost, reducing output towards the efficient level
raise the revenue needed to fund the government's provision of public goods
raise the profits earned by firms in the industry that pollute less than others
questions.explanation: A corrective tax adds the external cost to the producer's costs, so the market price better reflects social cost and the quantity falls towards the efficient level. Revenue is a by-product, not the market-failure reason for the tax.

questions.stem: A subsidy paid to producers of a good:
options: sets a legal minimum price for the good
lowers their costs, shifting supply to the right
raises their costs, shifting supply to the left
shifts the demand curve for the good to the right
questions.explanation: A subsidy is a payment that reduces producers' costs per unit, so they supply more at each price. The supply curve shifts right, lowering the price and raising the quantity traded.

questions.stem: The government subsidises the installation of rooftop solar panels. The market-failure reason for this is to:
options: raise the price of solar panels so that more firms enter the industry
correct the under-allocation of resources caused by positive externalities
correct an over-allocation of resources to the production of solar panels
provide solar panels because they are a pure public good for every household
questions.explanation: Rooftop solar reduces emissions that harm third parties, so its social benefit exceeds the private benefit and the market installs too few panels. A subsidy lowers the price and increases installations towards the efficient level.

questions.stem: A subsidy to childcare providers shifts the supply curve for childcare to the right. The likely result in the childcare market is:
options: a lower price and a smaller quantity traded
a higher price and a smaller quantity traded
a lower price and a larger quantity traded
a higher price and a larger quantity traded
questions.explanation: With demand unchanged, a rightward shift of supply moves the market down along the demand curve. The equilibrium price falls and the quantity traded rises.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of regulation used to address a market failure?
options: Running a national television campaign that promotes safe driving
Setting legal limits on the emissions a factory may release
Paying a grant to each firm that hires a new apprentice
Building a public library funded from tax revenue
questions.explanation: Regulation means rules backed by law that restrict or require certain behaviour. A grant is a subsidy, a public library is direct provision, and a television campaign is government advertising.

questions.stem: Fishing quotas that limit the catch of each licensed boat are mainly designed to address:
options: the overuse of a common access resource
the under-provision of a public good
asymmetric information between fishers and buyers
a positive consumption externality from eating fish
questions.explanation: Open fisheries are rival and non-excludable, so they tend to be overfished. Quotas limit the total catch, protecting fish stocks for the future.

questions.stem: A government advertising campaign warning of the health risks of vaping aims mainly to:
options: shift the supply of vaping products to the left by raising producers' costs of production
lower the price of vaping products so that fewer firms remain in the market
move consumers along the demand curve by raising the price of vaping products
shift demand for vaping products to the left by improving consumers' information
questions.explanation: Information campaigns work on the demand side: better-informed consumers want less of the product at every price. They do not change producers' costs or the product's price directly.

questions.stem: A weakness of government advertising as a way of correcting a market failure is that:
options: it can be used only when the good concerned is a public good
its effect on behaviour can be slow and difficult to measure
it directly raises the costs of production for the firms involved
it immediately raises the market price of the good being targeted
questions.explanation: Advertising relies on people changing their choices, which may take years and is hard to attribute to the campaign. It does not change firms' costs or the price directly.

questions.stem: Direct provision as a form of government intervention means that:
options: the government pays private firms a subsidy so they can lower their prices
the government sets rules about how a good may be produced and sold
the government taxes goods that harm third parties
the government itself supplies a good or service, often free or below cost
questions.explanation: Under direct provision the government produces or funds the good itself, as with public roads or national defence. Subsidies, regulations and taxes leave production to private firms.

questions.stem: Governments usually provide national defence directly because:
options: it creates negative externalities that can be corrected only by taxing private suppliers
private firms would over-provide it at too low a price for the public
demand for it is highly price elastic, so private firms would earn little
it is a public good, so private firms could not charge enough to cover its cost
questions.explanation: Defence protects everyone, whether or not they pay, so free riding means a private market would supply little or none of it. Direct provision funded by taxes solves the free-rider problem.

questions.stem: A government sets a maximum rent on rental housing below the equilibrium rent. A likely unintended consequence is:
options: a shortage of rental housing, as landlords offer fewer properties for rent
a surplus of rental properties that remain vacant for long periods
higher rents paid by tenants in the controlled part of the market
an increase in the number of new rental properties being built by investors
questions.explanation: A price ceiling below equilibrium raises the quantity demanded and lowers the quantity supplied, creating a shortage. Fewer homes are available than people want at the controlled rent, which reduces allocative efficiency.

questions.stem: A subsidy keeps an inefficient local manufacturer in business, shielding it from lower-cost competitors. The subsidy is most likely to reduce:
options: productive efficiency, as output stays with a higher-cost producer
intertemporal efficiency, as natural resources are used up faster
the quantity supplied, as the subsidy raises the firm's costs
consumers' access to the good, as the subsidy raises its price
questions.explanation: Resources stay with a firm that produces at a higher cost than its rivals, so the same output uses more resources than necessary. A subsidy lowers a firm's costs and price rather than raising them.

questions.stem: Lengthy approval processes for new medical devices are intended to protect patients, but they may unintentionally reduce:
options: allocative efficiency, by making medical devices non-excludable goods
dynamic efficiency, by slowing how quickly new products reach the market
intertemporal efficiency, by encouraging natural resources to be used up faster
productive efficiency, by lowering what it costs to make each device
questions.explanation: Long delays slow the speed at which resources move into new and better products, which is a loss of dynamic efficiency. Lowering production costs would raise productive efficiency, not reduce it.

questions.stem: Large increases in tobacco excise have been followed by growth in the sale of illegal tobacco. This illustrates that:
options: demand for tobacco is perfectly price elastic, so the tax had no effect on smoking
indirect taxes shift the demand curve for a taxed good to the right
the tax has fully corrected the externality from smoking
an intervention can have unintended consequences that offset part of its intended effect
questions.explanation: Higher legal prices create an incentive to supply untaxed tobacco, so some consumption moves to an illegal market rather than stopping. That weakens both the health effect and the revenue the tax was meant to deliver.

questions.stem: An intervention intended to correct a market failure leaves resources allocated less efficiently than before. Economists call this:
options: market failure
a positive externality
deregulation
government failure
questions.explanation: Government failure occurs when intervention makes resource allocation worse rather than better, often through unintended consequences. Market failure is the problem the intervention was meant to fix.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches a market failure with an intervention commonly used to address it?
options: Under-consumption of education — a regulation limiting enrolments
Pollution from a factory — a tax on each tonne of emissions
Under-provision of a public good — a tax on the good's consumers
Overuse of a common access resource — a subsidy to increase its use
questions.explanation: A tax on emissions makes polluters pay the external cost, reducing pollution towards the efficient level. Subsidising use of a common access resource would worsen overuse, and limiting enrolments would deepen the under-consumption of education.
